In nineteen ninety-four, a hundred and ninety-nine dog-show judges ranked the breeds. Border Collie, first. Afghan Hound, last.
Testing an animal's mind is tricky. Clever Hans, a horse, seemed to count. He was reading his questioner's tiny nods.
The judges ranked trainability. A top dog learns a new command in under five tries. A bottom dog may need a hundred.
Scientists test one skill at a time: following a pointing finger, or walking around a clear tube to reach the treat.
Breeds differ a lot in self-control, a little in reading people, and hardly at all in memory. There is no single dog IQ.
Breed says little about one dog. In eighteen thousand dogs, it explained about nine percent of behaviour.
Emotional skills are tested in pieces too. Dogs have a muscle that lifts the inner eyebrow. Fifteen of eighteen went to a crying person.
Cats are harder. Many walk away. At a box they can't open, most dogs look back at a human. Most cats keep trying.
Yet cats know their names, and two in three kittens bond securely, like human babies. No one has ranked cat breeds by intelligence.
So, which is smarter? Ask which skill, and which animal. The dog in front of you is mostly itself.
